newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand business confidence rebounds -- bank.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand business confidence rebounds -- bank.

text.p: New Zealand business confidence rebounded from pre-election jitters in November, the National Bank said on Friday in its latest monthly survey.
A net 20 percent of respondents expect general business conditions to improve over the coming year, reversing last month's dip and returning confidence back to September's level.
However, in a separate report, independent forecaster BERL predicted the economy would slow considerably in 1997/98 -- a forecast conflicting with those of most other forecasters.
National Bank said the confidence rebound was across all sectors with the largest turnaround in agriculture.
Confidence in that sector hit the positive for the first time since February but remains well below other sectors.

An unprecedented 65 percent of respondents expect interest rates to fall and this has triggered a big rise in construction intentions. Not since November 1993 have expectations on interest rates approached the present level.
"Residential construction intentions have bolted after a dose of the blues in the June quarter," chief economist Adrian Orr said.
Residential construction intentions have risen from a negative 37 percent in July to plus 22 percent.
Orr noted that short-term interest rates had already fallen one percentage point since mid-October and meanwhile "inevitable" increased government spending had been announced.
"These factors limit the scope for future interest rate declines," he said.
BERL is forecasting a further reduction in real GDP growth -- down to 1.2 percent in the March 1997 year and 1.0 percent for the following year, unless there is an easing in the exchange rate.
BERL said other economists are not fully recognising the effects flowing from tight monetary policies, namely the reduction in activity, job losses, and slack demand.
It noted full-time jobs in the tradeable sector had fallen 26,000 from April to September. It said the sector is in recession.
Public sector construction would prop up the economy in 1997/98 while consumer spending would be soft.
BERL said a further rise in the current account deficit from NZ$4 billion "must at some point be seen as unsustainable by the financial markets".
It expects that by the end of the 1997 winter the exchange rate will begin a 10 percent decline.
